extracted.intended_audience: military lawyers, judge advocates, legal scholars, and military officers concerned with martial law, occupation, and military commissions
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the legal authority, scope, composition, procedure, and limitations of military commissions and provisional military courts in occupied or insurrectionary territories. Covers when such tribunals may be convened, what offenses they may try, procedural norms, sentencing limits, and the relation to civilian courts and treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to create civil and criminal tribunals in occupied/conquered territory
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority to create courts with civil as well as criminal jurisdiction in a conquered country in military occupation attaches to the dominant power by the law of war and of nations as an incident to the power to establish a military government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: it is the right and duty of the conqueror to institute such courts 'for the security of persons and property and for the administration of justice.' When courts were created by commanding generals during the Civil War the order of the commander was presumed to be the order and act of the President. (Cites: Leitensdorfer v. Webb and related cases; discussion of Provost and Provisional Courts.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of provost/provisional court judgments by civil courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments rendered by provost or provisional courts established by competent military commanders have been recognized as lawful and enforceable by the civil courts (e.g., recognition by U.S. Supreme Court in Mechanics' & Traders' Bk. v. Union Bk., The Grapeshot, Burke v. Miltenberger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited where large civil judgments and admiralty jurisdiction were sustained; references to cases and reporter citations supporting legitimacy of such tribunals when properly constituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of military government to collect duties and exactions in occupied territory
rubrics_metrics.description: When military government is maintained within an enemy's country a military government may collect duties and no court can question a right to collect such duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: held that a tax of $5 per bale levied by a military commander at New Orleans (Gen. Canby) upon cotton and applied to hospital/sanitary/charitable purposes was authorized under discretionary wartime power. (C.6138, Apr. 12, 1899; R. 18, 668, Mar. 1866.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributions/exactions from the enemy justified by law of war
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions of money exacted from the enemy by competent military authority are justified by the law of war and conquest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative historical practice cited (assessments by Gen. Scott in 1847, etc.) and specific rulings recognizing such exactions when made under proper military authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of occupying military governor to deport persons for military reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: When the United States occupies hostile territory and places in charge a military governor he may, upon proper cause, deport from that hostile territory persons 'as a menace to the military situation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: C.10002, Mar. 18, 1901. Presents deportation as a permissible security measure under occupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military commissions as authorized wartime tribunals deriving authority from law of war
rubrics_metrics.description: Military commissions have become adopted as authorized tribunals in time of war; they are criminal war courts whose authority is derived from the law of war, though in some cases their powers have been added to by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice from 1847 onward, statutory references (Acts of Congress), executive proclamations, court rulings, and Attorney General opinions are cited to demonstrate acceptance and sources of authority. (G. O. orders, act of Mar.3,1863, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two primary classes of offenses within military commission jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A military commission is authorized to exercise jurisdiction over two classes of offenses: (1) Violations of the laws of war, and (2) Civil crimes which, because civil authority is superseded and civil courts closed or suspended, cannot be taken cognizance of by ordinary tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing explains why commissions try both war-specific offenses and ordinary crimes when civil courts are nonfunctional; citations to R. series decisions supporting both classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to try offenses committed before military government or before initiation of martial law
rubrics_metrics.description: A military commission, whether exercising jurisdiction under the laws of war or as a substitute for local criminal courts, may take cognizance of offenses committed during the war before the initiation of the military government or martial law, but not then brought to trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in various rulings (R. 19, 390, Jan. 1866); includes that enemy prisoners may be tried for violations committed before capture, subject to clear proof that the act was not a legitimate act of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal limit: commission jurisdiction continues until peace or formal termination of war status
rubrics_metrics.description: The jurisdiction of a military commission convened under the law of war may be exercised up to the date of a peace agreed upon between hostile parties or the declaration by competent authority of the termination of the war status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited rulings: R.20,484 (Mar.1866); various Comptroller decisions (C.6003, C.6286, etc.). Emphasizes that jurisdiction ceases with formal peace/termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction-act commissions: procedural form by military rules; jurisdiction/punishment by local statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Military commissions convened under the Reconstruction act (Mar.3,1867) are to be governed as to form of procedure by rules governing military commissions under the laws of war, while as to jurisdiction and power of punishment they are generally to be regulated by the local statutes governing the courts for which they are substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Advocate General's rulings (R.29,406, Nov.1869) explained practical operation: commissions could try offenses committed before the act, could not take cases within jurisdiction of U.S. courts in operation, and sentences approved by competent authority might be executed prior to state readmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military commissions cannot assume jurisdiction when civil courts are open
rubrics_metrics.description: In a State or district where military government or martial law has not prevailed, or has ceased and regular criminal courts are open and in operation, a military commission cannot be empowered to assume jurisdiction of a public offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple holdings cited (R.9,657 Sept.1864; 12,422 June 1865; etc.). Also applied a fortiori where at date of offense no state of war existed; e.g., commissions could not try Indians for ordinary raiding where no war existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: No jurisdiction over civil suits or private damages when convened under laws of war
rubrics_metrics.description: A military commission convened for the trial of offenses under the law of war has no jurisdiction of civil suits or proceedings either based upon contract or brought to recover damages for private transactions or personal injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited rulings (R.3,190 July 1863; R.5,86 Oct.1863; R.9,205 May 1864; etc.) emphasize separation between criminal wartime jurisdiction and civil litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation vis-à-vis courts-martial: cannot try offenses exclusively within court-martial jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where invested by statute with a jurisdiction concurrent with that of courts-martial (e.g., spies by Mar.3,1863), the authority of military commissions cannot be extended to the trial of offenses which are specifically or generally made cognizable and punishable by courts-martial by the Articles of War or other statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated instances during the Civil War where commissions improperly assumed jurisdiction over courts-martial matters were recommended for disapproval by Judge Advocate General (R. Series cited). Statutory concurrency is rare (section 1343 R.S. for spies noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to general courts-martial in constitution and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Because statute has not defined commission constitution/composition/procedure, the rules applicable to general courts-martial have ordinarily been applied to military commissions (same convening officers, similar charges and specifications, similar recordings and sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent shows commissions convened by same officers as courts-martial, proceedings recorded similarly; minimum membership fixed by usage at three; usual presence of a judge advocate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum composition and presence of judge advocate
rubrics_metrics.description: A military commission constituted with less than three members, or which proceeded to trial with less than three members, or which was not attended by a judge advocate, would be contrary to precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulings cited (R.9,591 Sept.1864; 11,479 Feb.1865; 13,286 Jan.1865; 15,204 May 1865; C.17328 Jan.4,1905). The minimum of members has been fixed by usage at three and commissions have generally been supplied with a judge advocate as prosecuting officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural protections: oath, challenges, voting thresholds, statute of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Military commissions should be sworn like general courts-martial; the accused should have the right of challenging their members; two-thirds of members should concur in death sentences; the two-years limitation (statute of limitations) should be applied to prosecutions before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.11,111 Nov.1864 (swearing); R.23,650 Aug.1867 (two-thirds for death); R.9,657 Sept.1864 (two years limitation); right to challenge and other procedural analogies reiterated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion and approval of commission proceedings by convening officer/successor
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings of a military commission should be completed by the action at the end thereof of the officer who convened the commission or by his successor in command, the mode of procedure being the same as is followed by general courts-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: C.5292 Nov.5,1898. Emphasizes continuity of convening authority's role and successor's authority to complete proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes and offenses triable by military commissions (war-specific and ordinary crimes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Military commissions have tried a wide variety of offenses: war-specific offenses (unauthorized trading with the enemy, correspondence, blockade running, manufacturing arms for enemy, furnishing contraband, recruiting for the enemy, guerrilla warfare, violating flags of truce, violating parole, etc.) and ordinary crimes (homicides, robbery, assault and battery, larceny, receiving stolen property, rape, arson, burglary, riot, bribery, embezzlement, defrauding the United States, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists many principal offenses prosecuted during the Civil War and later practice (R. series, multiple citations). Also notes combination charges (e.g., murder charged as violating laws of war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined offenses and charging 'murder in violation of the laws of war'
rubrics_metrics.description: Not unfrequently the crime charged combined war-specific and ordinary offenses (e.g., killing officers or soldiers after surrender or while held as prisoners of war charged as 'murder in violation of the laws of war').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and rulings cited (R.7,360 Mar.1864; 17,435 and 19,221 Oct.1860; 20,650 May 1866) showing convictions under combined theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentencing limits and character of punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in a spy case where the sentence must be death (sec.1343 R.S.), the discretion of the military commission in imposing sentence is not in terms restricted by existing law; the sentence should award a criminal punishment and not a judgment of debt or damages. When acting under reconstruction laws as substitute State criminal courts, the commission should generally take into consideration the State statute prescribing penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.3,190 July 1863 (no civil judgments); R.29,406 Nov.1869 and C.12397 Apr.10,1902 (consider State statutory penalties when acting as substitute). Typical punishments historically included imprisonment 'for a term or till the end of the war,' fines, sending beyond lines, confiscation, oaths of allegiance, paroles, bonds for future behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of peace or treaty on occupation and provisional courts
rubrics_metrics.description: After declaration of peace the rule of hostile occupation can no longer be enforced (example: Porto Rico), but if ordinary criminal courts cannot be relied upon to suppress crime the President has power to appoint provisional courts with competent jurisdiction to continue until Congress provides a system of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C.6003 Mar.9,1899; C.6286 Apr.13,1899. Also notes that a government established under military occupation may continue until Congress shall have made other provision and is not necessarily terminated by a treaty (C.25629 Sept.30,1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive duty and steps under treaty intervention clauses (U.S.–Cuba Article 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the treaty between the United States and Cuba (May 22,1903, art.3) the U.S. may exercise the right to intervene to preserve Cuban independence and maintain a government adequate to protect life, property, and liberty; the duty is primarily executive and may require political/advisory steps, proclamations, and, if necessary, employment of land and naval forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that intervention is an executive duty (C.20396 Sept.15,1906). Outlined steps: notify island authorities/undertake negotiations, issue proclamation calling insurgents to disperse within a specific date, then employ forces if pacific measures fail. Historical analogies and prior presidential proclamations are cited.
